## 17 **Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data**

### 17.1 Learning Outcome

By the end of this hands-on exercise you will be able create the followings data visualisation by using R packages:

-   plotting a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions,

-   plotting a cycle plot by using ggplot2 function,

-   plotting a slopegraph

-   plotting a horizon chart

### 17.2 Getting Started

### 17.3 Do It Yourself

Write a code chunk to check, install and launch the following R packages: scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes, gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table and tidyverse.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse, ggplot2)
```
:::


### **17.4 Plotting Calendar Heatmap**

In this section, you will learn how to plot a calender heatmap programmatically by using ggplot2 package.

![](17.4%20Plotting%20Calendar%20Heatmap.png){width="536"}

By the end of this section, you will be able to:

-   plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,

-   to write function using R programming,

-   to derive specific date and time related field by using base R and lubridate packages

-   to perform data preparation task by using tidyr and dplyr packages.

### **17.4.1 The Data**

For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, *eventlog.csv* file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.

### **17.4.2 Importing the data**

First, you will use the code chunk below to import *eventlog.csv* file into R environment and called the data frame as *attacks*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks <- read_csv("eventlog.csv")
```
:::


### 17.4.3 Examining the data structure

It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.

For example, *kable()* can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|timestamp           |source_country |tz              |
|:-------------------|:--------------|:---------------|
|2015-03-12 15:59:16 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:00:48 |FR             |Europe/Paris    |
|2015-03-12 16:02:26 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:02:38 |US             |America/Chicago |
|2015-03-12 16:03:22 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:03:45 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |


:::
:::


There are three columns, namely *timestamp*, *source_country* and *tz*.

-   *timestamp* field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.

-   *source_country* field stores the source of the attack. It is in *ISO 3166-1 alpha-2* country code.

-   *tz* field stores time zone of the source IP address.

![](17.4.3%20Timestamp.png)

### **17.4.4 Data Preparation**

Step 1: Deriving *weekday* and *hour of day* fields

Before we can plot the calender heatmap, two new fields namely *wkday* and *hour* need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}
```
:::


::: callout-note
-   [`ymd_hms()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/ymd_hms.html) and [`hour()`](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/reference/hour.html) are from [**lubridate**](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/) package, and

-   [`weekdays()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/weekdays) is a **base** R function.
:::

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
```
:::


::: callout-note
Beside extracting the necessary data into *attacks* data frame, `mutate()` of **dplyr** package is used to convert *wkday* and *hour* fields into **factor** so they’ll be ordered when plotting
:::

Table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|tz           |source_country |wkday    |hour |
|:------------|:--------------|:--------|:----|
|Africa/Cairo |BG             |Saturday |20   |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |6    |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |8    |
|Africa/Cairo |CN             |Sunday   |11   |
|Africa/Cairo |US             |Sunday   |15   |
|Africa/Cairo |CA             |Monday   |11   |


:::
:::


### **17.4.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL, 
     y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
-   a tibble data table called *grouped* is derived by aggregating the attack by *wkday* and *hour* fields.

-   a new field called *n* is derived by using `group_by()` and `count()` functions.

-   `na.omit()` is used to exclude missing value.

-   `geom_tile()` is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. `color` and `size` arguments are used to specify the border color and line size of the tiles.

-   [`theme_tufte()`](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/theme_tufte.html) of [**ggthemes**](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/index.html) package is used to remove unnecessary chart junk. To learn which visual components of default ggplot2 have been excluded, you are encouraged to comment out this line to examine the default plot.

-   `coord_equal()` is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.

-   `scale_fill_gradient()` function is used to creates a two colour gradient (low-high).
:::

![](17.4.5.png)

Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.

### **17.4.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

**Challenge:** Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.

![](17.4.6.png)

### **17.4.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

Step 1: Deriving attack by country object

In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, you are required to do the followings:

-   count the number of attacks by country,

-   calculate the percent of attackes by country, and

-   save the results in a tibble data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```
:::


Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame

In this step, you are required to extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from attacks data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. top4_attacks).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()
```
:::


### **17.4.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps**

Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calender Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### 17.5 Plotting Cycle Plot

In this section, you will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.

![](17.5.png)

### **17.5.1 Step 1: Data Import**

For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* will be used.

The code chunk below imports *arrivals_by_air.xlsx* by using `read_excel()` of **readxl** package and save it as a tibble data frame called *air*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air <- read_excel("arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
```
:::


### 17.5.2 Step 2: Deriving month and year fields

Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from Month-Year field.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))
```
:::


### **17.5.3 Step 3: Extracting the target country**

Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)
```
:::


### **17.5.4 Step 4: Computing year average arrivals by month**

The code chunk below uses `group_by()` and `summarise()` of **dplyr** to compute year average arrivals by month.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))
```
:::


### **17.5.5 Step 5: Plotting the cycle plot**

The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## 17.6 Plotting Slopegraph

In this section you will learn how to plot a [slopegraph](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/blog/2020/7/27/what-is-a-slopegraph) by using R.

Before getting start, make sure that **CGPfunctions** has been installed and loaded onto R environment. Then, refer to [Using newggslopegraph](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CGPfunctions/vignettes/Using-newggslopegraph.html) to learn more about the function. Lastly, read more about `newggslopegraph()` and its arguments by referring to this [link](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/CGPfunctions/versions/0.6.3/topics/newggslopegraph).

### **17.6.1 Step 1: Data Import**

Import the rice data set into R environment by using the code chunk below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rice <- read_csv("rice.csv")
```
:::


### **17.6.2 Step 2: Plotting the slopegraph**

Next, code chunk below will be used to plot a basic slopegraph as shown below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rice2 <- rice %>% 
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  mutate(
    Year = factor(Year, levels = c(1961, 1980)),
    x = as.numeric(Year)
  )

ggplot(rice2, aes(x = x, y = Yield, group = Country, colour = Country)) +
  geom_segment(
    data = rice2 %>% filter(Year == 1961),
    aes(x = 0.25, xend = 0.95, y = Yield, yend = Yield),
    colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = rice2 %>% filter(Year == 1980),
    aes(x = 2.05, xend = 2.75, y = Yield, yend = Yield),
    colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Yield), colour = "black", size = 2.5, vjust = -0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice2 %>% filter(Year == 1961),
    aes(x = 0.23, label = Country),
    colour = "black", fontface = "bold", hjust = 1, size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice2 %>% filter(Year == 1980),
    aes(x = 2.77, label = Country),
    colour = "black", fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("1961", "1980"),
    position = "top",
    limits = c(0.05, 2.95)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
    subtitle = "1961-1980",
    caption = "Prepared by: Dr. Kam Tin Seong",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
For effective data visualisation design, `factor()` is used convert the value type of *Year* field from numeric to factor.

Furthermore, there seems to be an issue with the library: newggslopegraph. Hence, we replaced it with ggplot.
:::

# Additional Analysis

## Additional Analysis 1 - Normalised Attack Timing Pattern by Top Source Countries

**Objective:** To compare the attack timing patterns of the top source countries by weekday and hour, after normalising attack volume within each country.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks_raw <- read_csv("eventlog.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

make_attack_time <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  utc_times <- ymd_hms(ts, tz = "UTC", quiet = TRUE)
  local_times <- with_tz(utc_times, tzone = tz[1])
  
  data.table(
    source_country = sc,
    wkday = weekdays(local_times),
    hour = hour(local_times)
  )
}

wkday_levels <- c("Saturday", "Friday", 
                  "Thursday", "Wednesday", 
                  "Tuesday", "Monday", 
                  "Sunday")

attacks_time <- attacks_raw %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_attack_time(.$timestamp,
                      .$source_country,
                      .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    wkday = factor(wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour = factor(hour, levels = 0:23)
  )

top6_country <- attacks_time %>%
  count(source_country, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  pull(source_country)

attack_hour_share <- attacks_time %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top6_country) %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(source_country, levels = top6_country)) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour, name = "attacks") %>%
  complete(source_country, wkday, hour, fill = list(attacks = 0)) %>%
  group_by(source_country) %>%
  mutate(share = attacks / sum(attacks)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(attack_hour_share,
       aes(hour, wkday, fill = share)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ source_country, ncol = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    name = "Share of attacks",
    low = "sky blue",
    high = "dark blue",
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Normalised Attack Timing Pattern of Top 6 Source Countries",
    subtitle = "Darker tiles show the weekday-hour combinations where each country is more active"
  ) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


**Insight:** The heatmap shows that attack activities are not evenly distributed across all countries. Some countries, such as KR, show more concentrated darker blocks during specific weekday-hour periods, suggesting stronger timing patterns. In contrast, countries such as CN and US appear more evenly spread across many hours.

## Additional Analysis 2 - Seasonality of Top Visitor Markets by Air

**Objective:** To examine whether the top visitor markets show recurring monthly seasonality in air arrivals from 2010 to 2019.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air <- read_excel("arrivals_by_air.xlsx")

air_tidy <- air %>%
  mutate(
    month = factor(month(`Month-Year`),
                   levels = 1:12,
                   labels = month.abb,
                   ordered = TRUE),
    year = year(`Month-Year`)
  ) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(`Month-Year`, month, year),
    names_to = "country",
    values_to = "arrivals"
  )

top4_markets <- air_tidy %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(total_arrivals = sum(arrivals, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total_arrivals)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 4) %>%
  pull(country)

market_cycle <- air_tidy %>%
  filter(country %in% top4_markets) %>%
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = top4_markets))

market_avg <- market_cycle %>%
  group_by(country, month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(arrivals, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = market_cycle,
    aes(x = year,
        y = arrivals,
        group = month),
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    data = market_avg,
    aes(yintercept = avgvalue),
    linetype = 6,
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  facet_grid(country ~ month, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonality of Top 4 Visitor Markets by Air, 2010-2019",
    subtitle = "Red dashed lines show the average arrivals for each month",
    x = NULL,
    y = "No. of Visitors"
  ) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 7, face = "bold")
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


**Insight:** The cycle plot shows clear seasonal differences across visitor markets. China shows strong growth over time, especially in months such as July and August. Indonesia has stronger arrivals around June, July, and December, suggesting possible holiday-driven travel patterns. Australia and Malaysia show more moderate but still visible seasonal movement.

## Additional Analysis 3: Rice Production Growth from 1980 to 2010

**Objective:** To compare how rice production changed across Asian countries between 1980 and 2010.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rice_prod <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1980, 2010)) %>%
  mutate(Production_mil = Production / 1000000) %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(
    change_mil = Production_mil[Year == 2010] -
                 Production_mil[Year == 1980]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    Year = factor(Year, levels = c(1980, 2010)),
    x = as.numeric(Year)
  )

ggplot(rice_prod,
       aes(x = x,
           y = Production_mil,
           group = Country,
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice_prod %>% filter(Year == 1980),
    aes(x = 0.75,
        label = paste0(Country, " (", round(Production_mil, 1), "m)")),
    colour = "black",
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = rice_prod %>% filter(Year == 2010),
    aes(x = 2.25,
        label = paste0(round(Production_mil, 1), "m")),
    colour = "black",
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("1980", "2010"),
    position = "top",
    limits = c(0.45, 2.55)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "m")) +
  labs(
    title = "Rice Production Growth of Asian Countries",
    subtitle = "Comparison between 1980 and 2010",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


**Insight:**  The slopegraph shows that China remained the largest rice producer, increasing from about 142.9 million to 197.2 million. India also increased strongly from about 80.3 million to 120.6 million. Among the smaller producers, Indonesia and Vietnam recorded strong growth.
